title: Danse macabre
hook: Midnight strikes, Death tunes his fiddle and the skeletons waltz until the cock crows, in seven minutes.

painting.title: Danse Macabre
painting.collection: Niguliste Museum, Art Museum of Estonia, Tallinn
painting.pairingNote: Skeletons lead a pope, an emperor, an empress, a cardinal and a king in a dance, while one of them plays the bagpipes; the poem behind Saint-Saëns’s piece makes the same point, that in Death’s dance everyone is equal.

facts: In 1872 Saint-Saëns set a short poem by Henri Cazalis as a song for voice and piano. In the poem, Death strikes a tomb with his heel at midnight, plays a dance tune on his violin, and the skeletons dance in their shrouds until the cock crows. The poem’s title is “Égalité, Fraternité”: in the dance, the lord and the peasant are the same.

In 1874 he turned the song into a [[symphonic-poem|symphonic poem]] for orchestra. The voice disappears, and Death’s violin becomes a real solo violin. The first performance was in Paris on 24 January 1875, conducted by Édouard Colonne.

The orchestra includes a xylophone, still a rarity in a symphony orchestra at the time, for the rattle of dry bones. Saint-Saëns borrowed the idea again in “Fossils” from *The Carnival of the Animals*.
The whole piece is a waltz, in three beats, in G minor. Two tunes carry it: a jerky one, first on the flute, and a sliding one on the violin.
bigPicture.inOneLine: midnight, Death tunes up, the dance starts quietly, grows wild, and stops dead at dawn.

movements.heading: Mouvement modéré de valse
movements.summary: One continuous movement, a story told in order. The harp strikes midnight, the solo violin tunes up with a harsh, out-of-tune chord, and two waltz tunes start the dance. They pass round the orchestra, are piled up against each other and grow louder, with a mocking quotation of an old funeral chant halfway through. At the height of the frenzy an oboe crows, the dance breaks off, and the dead slip back into their graves.

mainIdeas.name: The first waltz tune
mainIdeas.description: short, jerky phrases that keep falling, first on the flute, later rattled out by the xylophone.

mainIdeas.name: The second waltz tune
mainIdeas.description: a long, smooth line sliding down a scale, played by the solo violin over soft string chords.

mainIdeas.name: Death’s violin
mainIdeas.description: the soloist’s top string is tuned down a semitone, so the open strings sound A and E-flat together, a clashing interval old theorists called “the devil in music”. The retuning is called [[scordatura|scordatura]].

stops.hear: A harp plucks the same note twelve times, very softly, over hushed strings
Soft plucked notes in the low strings, then the solo violin plays a harsh, grating two-note chord again and again
stops.happening: Death taps the tomb with his heel and tunes his fiddle: the A and E-flat of the retuned violin

stops.hear: A flute plays a short, jerky tune over plucked strings, in waltz time
stops.happening: The first waltz tune. The dance begins, almost on tiptoe

stops.hear: The solo violin plays a long, smooth tune that slides down a scale
stops.happening: The second waltz tune, Death’s own melody

stops.hear: The dry, clicking sound of a xylophone joins the jerky tune
The sliding tune enters in one string section after another, each overlapping the last
stops.happening: A [[fugato|fugato]] on the second tune: the crowd of dancers grows

stops.hear: The woodwinds play a slow, solemn chant, but in a bright, skipping major key
stops.happening: The [[dies-irae|Dies irae]], the medieval chant of the Mass for the dead, turned into a joke

stops.hear: The violin returns with the dance; the tunes come back louder and faster
The whole orchestra, with brass, cymbals and xylophone, hammers out both tunes at full strength
stops.happening: The two waltz tunes together. The climax

stops.hear: A sudden break; the oboe plays a short, high call

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The solo violin plays a thin, sad fragment of its tune; soft plucked chords; a quiet ending
stops.happening: The dead hurry back to their graves

notice: Listen to the solo violin’s first chord. It sounds wrong on purpose: the instrument has been retuned so that Death’s fiddle grates.
The two waltz tunes start far apart, on the flute and the violin. Notice how, near the end, they sound at the same time.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Charles Dutoit recorded the piece with the Philharmonia Orchestra in Kingsway Hall, London, in 1980, for an album of Saint-Saëns’s four symphonic poems. On the Spotify album it is track 1, followed by *Phaéton* and *Le rouet d’Omphale*.

threads.title: A song without words
threads.body: The piece follows Cazalis’s poem line by line: the twelve strokes, the heel on the tomb, the violin, the skeletons, the cock. The voice is gone, but the story is all there.

threads.title: One idea, many colours
threads.body: Saint-Saëns builds seven minutes from two short waltz tunes. What changes is the orchestra: flute, violin, xylophone, a crowd of strings, then everyone at once.

threads.title: Death made light
threads.body: The subject is grim, but the tone is ironic: a waltz, a cheeky Dies irae, a rooster. The fear is part of the fun.
